claim: The projection from layer 5 neurons of the neocortex to the dorsal raphe nucleus undergoes a dramatic increase in synaptic potency between postnatal weeks 3 and 8 in mice.
source: Using optogenetic-assisted circuit mapping, we show that this projection undergoes a dramatic increase in synaptic potency between postnatal weeks 3 and 8, corresponding to the transition from juvenile to adult.
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing increased connection probability and amplitude of cortico-raphe input between weeks 3 and 8, as shown in Figure 1B, C.

claim: Behavioral persistence in mice increases during the same developmental period (postnatal weeks 3 to 8) when cortical input to the dorsal raphe nucleus matures.
source: We then show that this period corresponds to an increase in the behavioral persistence that mice exhibit in a foraging task.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data showing that adult mice (7-8 weeks) are more persistent than juvenile mice (3-4 weeks) in a probabilistic foraging task, as shown in Figure 2D-F.

claim: Selective ablation of the cortical pathway to the dorsal raphe nucleus in adult mice causes them to revert to a behavioral phenotype similar to juveniles.
source: Finally, we used a genetic targeting strategy that primarily affected neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex, to selectively ablate this pathway in adulthood and show that mice revert to a behavioral phenotype similar to juveniles.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral data showing that Caspase-treated mice exhibit reduced persistence similar to juvenile mice, as shown in Figure 3E-G.

claim: Frontal cortical to dorsal raphe input is a critical anatomical and functional substrate of the development and manifestation of behavioral persistence.
source: These results suggest that frontal cortical to dorsal raphe input is a critical anatomical and functional substrate of the development and manifestation of behavioral persistence.
evidence: The claim is based on the combined findings of developmental maturation of the pathway, behavioral changes during development, and the effects of pathway ablation.

claim: At 3-4 weeks (juvenile mice), the probability of DRN neurons receiving cortical input was 0.07.
source: At 3–4 weeks (juvenile mice), the probability of DRN neurons receiving cortical input was equal to 0.07.
evidence: The claim is directly supported by electrophysiological recordings quantifying connection probability.

claim: The connection probability of cortical input to DRN neurons increased significantly to 0.66 at weeks 5-6.
source: This probability increased significantly to 0.66 (Pcon 3–4 weeks vs. Pcon 5–6 weeks, Chi-square test χ2 (1, N = 52 neurons) = 24.1, p = 0.00001) at weeks 5–6
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical analysis showing a significant increase in connection probability.

claim: The connection probability of cortical input to DRN neurons reached a peak of 0.82 at weeks 7-8.
source: reaching a peak connection probability of 0.82 at weeks 7–8 (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings quantifying connection probability at different developmental stages.

claim: The amplitude of optogenetically evoked currents in DRN neurons increased from 27.3 ± 6.2 pA to 128 ± 15.7 pA between 5-6 and 7-8 weeks.
source: Between 5–6 and 7–8 weeks (i.e. late juvenile to adult mice), the amplitude of the optogenetically evoked currents increased from 27.3 ± 6.2 to 128 ± 15.7 pA (mean ± standard error of the mean [SEM], two-tailed t-test, t(55) = 4.03, p = 0.002).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of evoked postsynaptic currents.

claim: There is no further increase in connection probability or input magnitude between 7-8 weeks and 5-6 months of age.
source: We observed no further increase in either the connection probability (Pcon 7–8 weeks = 0.82 vs. Pcon 5–6 months = 0.80, Chi-square test χ2 (1, N = 70 neurons) = 0.03, p = 0.84) or the input magnitude (7–8 weeks old = 126 ± 15 pA vs. 5–6 months old = 113 ± 14.1 pA, two-tailed t-test, t(55) = 1.27, p = 0.21, Figure 2B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings and statistical comparisons showing no significant differences between these age groups.

claim: The cortico-raphe pathway gradually matures between weeks 3 and 8 and then plateaus.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that the cortico-raphe pathway gradually matures between weeks 3 and 8 and then plateaus.
evidence: The claim is based on the pattern of connection probability and amplitude changes across developmental stages.

claim: The location of recorded DRN neurons was comparable between juvenile and adult mice.
source: Importantly, the location of the recorded DRN neurons was comparable between juvenile and adult mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical analysis of recording locations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The passive electrical properties of DRN neurons did not change over development.
source: Furthermore, the passive electrical properties did not change over development, as measured by input resistance (3–4 weeks: median = 444 MΩ, 95% confidence interval [CI] = [370, 676], 5–6 weeks: median = 612 MΩ, 95% CI = [402, 925], 7–8 weeks: median = 731 MΩ, 95% CI = [519, 943], 5–6 months: median = 532 MΩ, 95% CI = [385, 664], Kruskal–Wallis H(3) = 6.06, p = 0.11) and input capacitance (3–4 weeks: median = 20.7 pF, 95% CI = [17.4, 25.9], 5–6 weeks: median = 22.8 pF, 95% CI = [15.9, 24.8], 7–8 weeks: median = 20.8 pF, 95% CI = [18.3, 28.5], 5–6 months: median = 23.5 pF, 95% CI = [14.1, 44.7], Kruskal–Wallis H(3) = 0.81, p = 0.84) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A, B)
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of input resistance and capacitance across developmental stages.

claim: Changes in passive propagation of current through DRN neurons is not the underlying cause of the apparent increase in connection probability and input magnitude observed over time.
source: suggesting that changes in the passive propagation of current through DRN neurons is not the underlying cause of the apparent increase in connection probability and input magnitude observed over time.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of changes in passive electrical properties across development.

claim: There is a significantly higher density of Rbp4 positive axons around the DRN in adults compared to juveniles.
source: Indeed, we observed a significantly higher density of Rbp4 positive axons around the DRN in adults compared to juveniles (2.2 ± 0.47 vs. 5.7 ± 0.56 axons per bin in juvenile vs. adult mice, two-tailed t-test (N Juveniles = 4, N Adults = 7), t(9) = 4.15, p = 0.002, Figure 1D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical quantification of axonal density shown in Figure 1D, E.

claim: The increase in physiological strength of cortico-raphe connections reflects in part the growth of new connections between the neocortex and DRN.
source: This observation supports the idea that the increase in physiological strength we observed reflects in part the growth of new connections between the neocortex and DRN.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between increased axonal density and increased synaptic strength.

claim: Cortico-accumbens projections did not undergo any significant structural change over the same developmental period (weeks 3-8).
source: In contrast to cortico-raphe afferents, cortico-accumbens projections did not undergo any significant structural change over the same developmental period (4.5 ± 0.54 vs. 5.8 ± 0.74 axons per bin in juvenile vs. adult mice, two-tailed t-test (N Juveniles = 3, N Adults = 7), t(8) = 1.09, p = 0.40, Figure 1D, E).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical quantification showing no significant difference in axonal density between juvenile and adult mice.

claim: There is no change in connection probability of cortico-accumbens connections between juvenile and adult mice.
source: Consistent with the anatomy, the ChR2-assisted mapping of cortico-accumbens connections in juvenile and adult Rbp4-ChR2 mice revealed no change in either the connection probability (Pcon 3–4 weeks = 0.90 vs. Pcon 7–8 weeks = 0 .87, Chi-square test χ2 (1, N = 19 neurons) = 0.03, p = 0.81) or the input amplitude in the transition from juveniles to adults (two-tailed t-test, t(15) = 0.15, p = 0.88, Figure 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing no significant changes in connection probability or amplitude.

claim: The structural and synaptic development of cortical afferents targeting the DRN during the transition to adulthood does not reflect a generalized development of corticofugal projections.
source: Altogether, these observations reveal the structural and synaptic development of a subpopulation of cortical afferents targeting the DRN during the transition to adulthood in mice that does not reflect a generalized development of corticofugal projections.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparison showing that cortico-raphe projections develop while cortico-accumbens projections do not.

claim: Juvenile and adult mice obtained a comparable reward rate in the foraging task.
source: Both groups obtained a comparable reward rate (Figure 2C; Adults: median = 0.02 rewards per second, 95% CI = [0.0020, 0.003], Juveniles: median = 0.023 rewards per second, 95% CI = [0.001, 0.012]; Mann–Whitney U test (N Adults = 21, N Juveniles = 23) = 82.0, p = 0.16)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral measurements showing no significant difference in reward rate between groups.

claim: Juveniles and adults do not differ in terms of overall competence in performing the foraging task.
source: indicating that juveniles and adults do not differ in terms of overall competence in performing the task.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparable reward rates obtained by both groups.

claim: For naive mice, elapsed time has more explanatory power on leaving decisions than the number of pokes.
source: Indeed, we found that contrary to trained mice (Vertechi et al., 2020), for naive mice, elapsed time has more explanatory power on leaving decisions (Akaike information criterion test Leave~1 + PokeTime + (1 + PokeTime|MouseID) vs. Leave~1 + PokeNumber + (1 + PokeNumber|MouseID): AICtime = 1.13e4, AICnumber = 1.14e4 p: 1.94e−23).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical model comparison using Akaike information criterion.

claim: Juveniles are significantly more likely to leave earlier than adults and thus are less persistent.
source: This analysis showed that juveniles are significantly more likely to leave earlier than adults and thus, less persistent (Figure 2D, E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by logistic regression analysis showing a significant effect of age on leaving probability.

claim: Including the Age group in the model significantly contributes to the ability to explain leaving decisions.
source: Consistently, including the Age group in the model significantly contributes to the ability to explain leaving decisions (likelihood ratio test on Leave~1 + PokeTime + Trial + Age + PokeTime&Age + Trial&Age + (1 + PokeTime + Trial|MouseID) vs. Leave~1 + PokeTime + Trial + (1 + PokeTime + Trial|MouseID): X2(3) = 15.65, p = 0.0013).
evidence: The claim is supported by likelihood ratio test comparing nested models.

claim: Throughout the session, animals progressively leave earlier, indicating they become less persistent over the course of the session.
source: We found that throughout the session animals were progressively leaving earlier — the probability of leaving increased as a function of Trial, indicating that animals become less persistent over the course of the session (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, likelihood ratio test on Leave~1 + PokeTime + Trial + Age + PokeTime&Age + Trial&Age +(1 + PokeTime + Trial|MouseID) vs. Leave~1 + PokeTime + Age + PokeTime&Age + (1 + PokeTime|MouseID): X2(−5) = 26.88, p < 1e−5).
evidence: The claim is supported by logistic regression analysis showing a significant effect of trial number on leaving probability.

claim: The decrease in persistence over trials is likely reflecting a drop in motivation due to the water drunk during the session or accumulated tiredness.
source: This is likely reflecting a drop in motivation due to the water drunk during the session or accumulated tiredness.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the cause of the observed behavioral change over trials.

claim: There was no significant interaction between Trial and Age factors.
source: Crucially, there was no significant interaction between Trial and Age factors (Figure 2E)
evidence: The claim is supported by logistic regression analysis showing no significant interaction effect.

claim: Differences in satiety or fatigue accumulated throughout the session do not underlie the change in persistence between juveniles and adults.
source: indicating that differences in satiety or fatigue accumulated throughout the session do not underlie the change in persistence between juveniles and adults.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of interaction between trial and age factors.

claim: Adults made more pokes per trial than juveniles.
source: Adults made more pokes per trial than juveniles (Figure 2F; Adults: median = 3.65 pokes per trial, 95% CI = [0.42, 0.51], Juveniles: median = 2.92 pokes per trial, 95% CI = [0.35, 0.50]; Mann–Whitney U test (N Adults = 21, N Juveniles = 23) = 354.5, p = 0.008, effect size = 0.73)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral measurements showing a significant difference in pokes per trial.

claim: Adults made more consecutive failures after the last reward than juveniles.
source: and more consecutive failures after the last reward Figure 2F; Adults: median = 2.69 pokes after last reward, 95% CI = [0.39, 0.53], Juveniles: median = 1.96 pokes after last reward, 95% CI = [0.41, 0.52]; Mann–Whitney U test (N Adults = 21, N Juveniles = 23) = 351.0, p = 0.009, effect size = 0.73.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral measurements showing a significant difference in consecutive pokes after last reward.

claim: Adult animals were consistently poking for longer than juveniles.
source: We found that adult animals were consistently poking for longer than juveniles, as indicated by both a significant effect of the Age variable (Figure 2H) and significant improvement in explanatory power with the Age factor: likelihood ratio test on Occupancy~1 + PokeTime + Age + Age&PokeTime + (1 + PokeTime|MouseID) vs. Occupancy~1 + PokeTime +(1 + PokeTime|MouseID), X2(2) = 20.10, p < 1e−4.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of port occupancy showing a significant effect of age.

claim: The difference in port occupancy between adults and juveniles was constant throughout the trial.
source: Furthermore, the difference between the two groups was constant throughout the trial, as shown by the lack of a significant interaction between poke time and age factors (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis showing no significant interaction effect.

claim: Adult animals are actively more persistent than juveniles and this is not explained by qualitative differences in their poking behavior.
source: Altogether these results indicate that adult animals are actively more persistent than juveniles and this is not explained by qualitative differences in their poking behavior.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined behavioral measurements showing increased pokes, consecutive failures, and port occupancy in adults.

claim: Sex had no significant effect on the probability of leaving either alone or in interaction with animals' age.
source: We found no significant effect of Sex on the probability of leaving either alone or in interaction with animals' age (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: The claim is supported by logistic regression analysis showing no significant effect of sex.

claim: Including Sex as a predictor had no significant improvement in the model's ability to explain the decision to leave.
source: and including Sex as a predictor had no significant improvement in the model's ability to explain the decision to leave (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, likelihood ratio test on Leave~1 + PokeTime + Trial + Age + Sex + Age&Sex + (1 + PokeTime + Trial|MouseID) vs. Leave~1 + PokeTime + Trial + Age + (1 + PokeTime + Trial|MouseID): X2(2) = 3.46, p = 0.18).
evidence: The claim is supported by likelihood ratio test comparing nested models.

claim: The maturation of persistence occurs at a similar rate in male and female mice.
source: These results indicate that the maturation of persistence occurs at a similar rate in male and female mice.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of sex effects on leaving decisions.

claim: The same density of tdTomato expressing somas was detected in the mPFC of juvenile and adult Rbp4-Cre/tdTomato-loxP mice.
source: The same density of tdTomato expressing somas was detected in the mPFC of juvenile and adult Rbp4-Cre/tdTomato-loxP mice (Juveniles: median = 4.59 somas per 0.01 mm2, 95% CI = [4.59, 6.18], vs. Adults: median = 5.22 somas per 0.01 mm2, 95% CI = [4.35, 6.06], Mann–Whitney U test (N Juveniles = 3, N Adults = 4) = 6, p = 0.99, Figure 1—figure supplement 2C)
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical quantification of tdTomato-expressing neurons.

claim: A comparable number of neurons underwent Cre-dependent recombination of the tdTomato fluorescent reporter under the control of the Rbp4 promoter at both juvenile and adult developmental time points.
source: indicating that a comparable number of neurons underwent a Cre-dependent recombination of the tdTomato fluorescent reporter under the control of the Rbp4 promoter at both developmental time points.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparable density of tdTomato-expressing neurons in juvenile and adult mice.

claim: Layer 5 neurons in the mPFC expressing ChR2 under the Rbp4 promoter produced the same amount of photocurrent upon light stimulation in juvenile and adult mice.
source: In agreement with the previous control, layer 5 neurons in the mPFC expressing ChR2 under the Rbp4 promoter produced the same amount of photocurrent upon light stimulation in juvenile and adult mice (repeated measures analysis of variance [ANOVA], F(1, 11) = 0. 138, p = 0.71 for age factor, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by electrophysiological measurements of photocurrents in ChR2-expressing neurons.

claim: Juvenile and adult mice have similar densities of cortical layer 5 projection neurons that could give rise to DRN afferents.
source: These experiments show that juvenile and adult mice have similar densities of cortical layer 5 projection neurons that could give rise to DRN afferents
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comparable densities of tdTomato-expressing neurons and similar photocurrents in juvenile and adult mice.

claim: Cortical layer 5 projection neurons in juvenile and adult mice express similar amounts of ChR2.
source: and that these neurons express similar amounts of ChR2 and thus, if present, projections should be equally detectable by optogenetic circuit mapping across ages.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the similar photocurrents evoked in ChR2-expressing neurons in juvenile and adult mice.

claim: The ablation approach primarily affected mPFC–DRN-projecting neurons, particularly from the PL/IL and AC cortices.
source: These observations suggest that our ablation approach primarily affected mPFC–DRN-projecting neurons, particularly from the PL/IL and AC cortices.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the anatomical analysis showing the highest density of tdTomato+ neurons and greatest neuronal loss in PL/IL and AC cortices.

claim: The PL/IL and AC cortices showed more extensive neuron density loss in caspase-injected mice.
source: and consistently more extensive neuron density loss in caspase-injected mice, quantified using the pan-neuronal marker NeuN (Figure 3A–C, control n = 8 mice vs. caspase n = 7 mice, two-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnoff test = 0.028, p = 0.002 for PL/IL and D = 0.024, p = 0.01 for AC).
evidence: The claim is supported by anatomical quantification of NeuN-expressing neurons showing significant loss in caspase-treated mice.

claim: Caspase mice and tdTomato control mice obtained a similar reward rate in the foraging task.
source: First, we confirmed that both groups could perform the task comparatively well, obtaining a similar reward rate (Figure 3E; tdTomato: median = 0.033 rewards per second, 95% CI = [0.019, 0.003], Caspase: median = 0.034 rewards per second, 95% CI = [0.010, 0.008]; Mann–Whitney U test (N tdTomato = 8, N Caspase = 7) = 21.0, p = 0.46).
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral measurements showing no significant difference in reward rate.

claim: Caspase mice made significantly fewer pokes per trial than tdTomato control mice.
source: However, in line with our observations in juvenile mice, we observed that Caspase mice made significantly fewer pokes per trial (Figure 3E; tdTomato: median = 3.99 pokes per trial, 95% CI = [1.15, 0.98], Caspase: median = 2.80 pokes per trial, 95% CI = [0.47, 0.54]; Mann–Whitney U test (N Caspase = 7, N tdTomato = 8) = 49, p = 0.014, effect size = 0.88)
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral measurements showing a significant difference in pokes per trial.

claim: Caspase mice made significantly lower number of pokes after last reward than tdTomato control mice.
source: and significantly lower number of pokes after last reward (Figure 3E; tdTomato: median = 3.01 pokes after last reward, 95% CI = [1.16, 0.98], Caspase: median = 1.87 pokes after last reward, 95% CI = [0.49, 0.44]; Mann–Whitney U test (N Caspase = 7, N tdTomato = 8) = 48, p = 0.02, effect size = 0.86) when compared to tdTomato controls.
evidence: The claim is supported by behavioral measurements showing a significant difference in consecutive pokes after last reward.

claim: Animals lacking cortico-raphe projections were significantly more likely to leave the patch earlier than control animals.
source: We therefore applied logistic regression analysis to test this difference and assess how this effect relates to the factors previously identified in the age comparison. Animals lacking cortico-raphe projections were significantly more likely to leave the patch earlier than control animals (Figure 3F, G).
evidence: The claim is supported by logistic regression analysis showing a significant effect of virus treatment on leaving probability.

claim: Including the Virus factor significantly improved the model performance for explaining leaving decisions.
source: Congruently, including the Virus factor significantly improved the model performance (likelihood ratio test on Leave~1 + PokeTime + Trial + Virus + PokeTime&Virus + Trial&Virus +( 1 +P okeTime + Trial|MouseID) vs. Leave~1 + PokeTime + Trial + (1 +P okeTime + Trial|MouseID): X2(3) = 10.83, p = 0.012).
evidence: The claim is supported by likelihood ratio test comparing nested models.

claim: The effects of satiety and tiredness did not differ between caspase and tdTomato infected groups.
source: Crucially, these effects did not differ between caspase and tdTomato infected groups, as shown by the lack of interaction between the trial and group factors (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by regression analysis showing no significant interaction between trial and virus factors.

claim: Caspase mice showed a shift toward shorter port occupancy.
source: As with the case of juvenile versus adult mice, Caspase mice showed a shift toward shorter port occupancy (Figure 3H).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of port occupancy data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: The viral intervention significantly impacted port occupancy.
source: A regression analysis showed that the viral intervention impacted significantly port occupancy (likelihood ratio test on Occupancy~1 + PokeTime + Virus + Virus&PokeTime +( 1 + PokeTime|MouseID) vs. Occupancy~1 + PokeTime + (1 + PokeTime|MouseID), X2(2) = 12 .69, p = 0.018)
evidence: The claim is supported by likelihood ratio test comparing nested models.

claim: Turning off the cortical input to the DRN makes adult mice behave more like juvenile mice when performing the foraging task.
source: Together, these results show that turning off the cortical input to the DRN, which mostly originates in the mPFC, makes adult mice behave more like juvenile mice when they are performing the same foraging task.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the behavioral similarities between caspase-treated adult mice and naive juvenile mice.

claim: Mature cortico-DRN innervation may be necessary for adult mice to be persistent in their behavior.
source: This suggests that mature cortico-DRN innervation may be necessary for adult mice to be persistent in their behavior, and this pathway may help mice learn to be persistent in their behavior.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the effects of pathway ablation on behavioral persistence.

claim: The cortico-raphe pathway may help mice learn to be persistent in their behavior.
source: This suggests that mature cortico-DRN innervation may be necessary for adult mice to be persistent in their behavior, and this pathway may help mice learn to be persistent in their behavior.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the developmental maturation of the pathway and its effects on behavior.

claim: In humans, adolescence spans from years ~10 to 18 of life.
source: which in humans spans from years ~10 to 18 of life and in mice from weeks ~3 to 8 of life
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about human development.

claim: In mice, adolescence spans from weeks ~3 to 8 of life.
source: which in humans spans from years ~10 to 18 of life and in mice from weeks ~3 to 8 of life
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about mouse development, supported by citation (Bell, 2018).

claim: Adolescence is a period of intense somatic maturation, including sexual development.
source: and is a period of intense somatic maturation, including sexual development (Bell, 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Bell, 2018.

claim: Adolescence correlates with a decrease in impulsive behavior characteristic of the juvenile phase.
source: and that correlates with a decrease in impulsive behavior characteristic of the juvenile phase (Rosati et al., 2023; Doremus-Fitzwater et al., 2012; Hammond et al., 2011; Konstantoudaki et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The mPFC undergoes intense postnatal maturation from childhood to adulthood, particularly during adolescence.
source: Crucially, the mPFC undergoes intense postnatal maturation from childhood to adulthood, particularly during adolescence (Chini and Hanganu-Opatz, 2021)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Chini and Hanganu-Opatz, 2021.

claim: The maturation of the mPFC includes structural and functional modifications during childhood and adolescence.
source: The maturation of the mPFC includes structural and functional modifications during childhood and adolescence (Chini and Hanganu-Opatz, 2021; Sakurai and Gamo, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: It has been long hypothesized that the neural changes occurring in the mPFC during development are central to the emergence of behavioral control.
source: Although it has been long hypothesized that the neural changes occurring in the mPFC during development are central to the emergence of behavioral control (e.g. Durston and Casey, 2006; Sowell et al., 1999)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous hypotheses in the literature.

claim: The specific plastic arrangements underlying behavioral control development remain poorly understood.
source: the specific plastic arrangements underlying behavioral control development remain poorly understood.
evidence: The claim represents a gap in current knowledge that motivates the study.

claim: Changes in cortical thickness caused by cellular structural plasticity and synaptic pruning are characteristic of early postnatal developmental phases in both humans and mice.
source: A number of studies have focused on the local changes of mPFC circuits, such as the changes in cortical thickness caused by cellular structural plasticity and synaptic pruning that are characteristic of early postnatal developmental phases in both humans and mice (Nagy et al., 2004; Alexander-Bloch et al., 2013; Ueda et al., 2015; Kolk and Rakic, 2022)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The development of mPFC afferents to the amygdala may shape the response to threats across different stages of development.
source: In particular, the development of mPFC afferents to the amygdala may shape the response to threats across different stages of development (Arruda-Carvalho et al., 2017; Dincheva et al., 2015; Gee et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The development of mPFC input onto the dorsal raphe nucleus shapes the response to stress.
source: and the development of mPFC input onto the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN) shapes the response to stress (Soiza-Reilly et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Soiza-Reilly et al., 2019.

claim: 5-HT neuron activity in the DRN is related to increases in the ability to wait for rewards.
source: A growing body of evidence supports that 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) neuron activity in the DRN is related to increases in the ability to wait for rewards (Winstanley et al., 2005; Fonseca et al., 2015; Lottem et al., 2018; Miyazaki et al., 2011; Miyazaki et al., 2018; Miyazaki et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The ability to wait for rewards can be considered an instance of behavioral or cognitive control.
source: This kind of behavior can be considered an instance of behavioral or cognitive control (Cools et al., 2008; Dayan and Huys, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Behavioral control can be manifested either as passive waiting or active persistence.
source: which can be manifested either as passive waiting (Fonseca et al., 2015; Miyazaki et al., 2012;Miyazaki et al., 2018; Miyazaki et al., 2014) or active persistence (Lottem et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The raphe has been implicated in the active overcoming of adverse situations.
source: The raphe has likewise been implicated in the active overcoming of adverse situations (Nishitani et al., 2019; Ohmura et al., 2020; Warden et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The mPFC sends a dense glutamatergic projection to the DRN at the adult stage.
source: The mPFC sends a dense glutamatergic projection to the DRN at the adult stage (Pollak Dorocic et al., 2014; Weissbourd et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: mPFC input can bidirectionally modulate the activity of 5-HT DRN neurons through monosynaptic excitation or disynaptic feedforward inhibition through local interneurons.
source: which can bidirectionally modulate the activity of 5-HT DRN neurons through monosynaptic excitation or disynaptic feedforward inhibition through local interneurons (Challis et al., 2014; Geddes et al., 2016; Maier, 2015; Warden et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Selective optogenetic activation of the mPFC inputs to the DRN elicits active behavioral responses in a challenging context.
source: Selective optogenetic activation of the mPFC inputs to the DRN elicits active behavioral responses in a challenging context (Warden et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Warden et al., 2012.

claim: Perturbations in the development of the mPFC-DRN pathway lead to maladaptive anxiety levels.
source: and perturbations in the development of this pathway lead to maladaptive anxiety levels (Soiza-Reilly et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Soiza-Reilly et al., 2019.

claim: Optogenetic activation of the DRN 5-HT input to the mPFC specifically promotes waiting for probabilistic rewards.
source: Conversely, optogenetic activation of the DRN 5-HT input to the mPFC specifically promotes waiting for probabilistic rewards (Miyazaki et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Miyazaki et al., 2020.

claim: There is reciprocal connectivity between the mPFC and DRN.
source: Given the reciprocal connectivity between the mPFC and DRN (Puig and Gulledge, 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Puig and Gulledge, 2011.

claim: Both mPFC and DRN causally modulate animals' ability to wait for delayed rewards.
source: and that both areas causally modulate animals' ability to wait for delayed rewards (Ciaramelli et al., 2021; Fonseca et al., 2015; Miyazaki et al., 2011; Miyazaki et al., 2018; Murakami et al., 2017; Schweighofer et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The maturation of mPFC input to the DRN over development could underlie the emergence of behavioral persistence in mice.
source: it seems plausible that the maturation of mPFC input to the DRN over development could underlie the emergence of behavioral persistence in mice.
evidence: The claim is a hypothesis based on the convergence of evidence from previous studies.
